turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on through. Sorry to keep you, the clinic's been hectic.
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He was getting ratty out there. That telly doesn't help.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): I can't hear myself think with it on. I'm shattered. Can we start.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. What's brought you in today?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): The waterworks. Up and down all night, and I feel like a wet rag by morning.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): How many times a night, roughly?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Err, five. No. Three or four. I lose count half asleep.
[SEG0008] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Four, most nights, and he...
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Let me speak.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Of course. How's the stream itself?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Weak. Stops and starts, then dribbles. Takes an age.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any burning when you pass water?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No burning.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the urine?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): No blood. I'd have come in shouting.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has this been going on?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm, I was going to say...
[SEG0018] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Not a fortnight. Don't let him say that.
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Six months. No, scratch that. It's a year of getting up three or four times a night, and the weak stream the same. A full year.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Through the day, any sudden urge where you've got to go straight away?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. Not the whole day, but when it comes I don't hang about.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): What do you drink in the evening?
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): Tea. Pot after the news, two or three mugs. Strong.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does that late tea make the nights worse?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Probably, yeah.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any backache, fever, or weight coming off?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): No. None of that. Just the tiredness.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Chest is fine.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bowels and appetite all right?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. Normal. No change.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you taking?
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): Ramipril, for the blood pressure. Two and a half milligrams... no, five. Five milligrams every morning.
[SEG0034] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And atorvastatin forty milligrams, with his tea... with his dinner, sorry.
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): Dinner. Yeah, forty milligrams.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or anything else?
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): Gave up twenty years ago. No, thirty years. Was twenty a day back then.
[SEG0040] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's let the allotment go. Used to be down there every day.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): I've overdone it down there for years. Anyway. Frog in my throat trying to get the words out, it's not a throat thing. Stick to the peeing.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll check your blood pressure. One thirty six over eighty four, and your pulse is seventy two.
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): Last time the nurse reckoned one fifty something. Made a right fuss.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll go with today's. Your abdomen is soft, no tenderness, and the bladder isn't palpable. I'll leave the prostate exam for another day.
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): Right. Not today.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working impression is lower urinary tract symptoms from a benign enlarged prostate. That's not a confirmed diagnosis, just where this is pointing.
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): You're not calling it cancer, then.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not, but I can't properly rule a prostate cancer out until the PSA is back.
[SEG0049] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His brother had prostate trouble. Had an operation. Wasn't cancer, they said.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you. We'll do a PSA blood test, and a urine test for blood and infection. Both are booked at reception before you go.
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): What, a sample today? I'll try. No promises.

[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's fine. I'm also starting tamsolusin, tamsulosin, sorry. Two hundred micrograms, no, four hundred micrograms, once a day, after food. Should help the stream and the dribbling.
[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): Another tablet. Will it flatten me? I feel like a wet rag as it is.

[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): It shouldn't make you drowsy. It can make you light-headed on standing, more so with the ramipril for your blood pressure. Stand up slowly. If you feel faint, leave it off and ring the surgery.
[SEG0055] person_3 (PATIENT): And what about the tea, then?
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Last mug around seven in the evening, not a pot after the news. That often knocks off one night-time trip.
[SEG0057] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And if he can't pee at all before we're back?
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you can't pass urine, or you see blood, don't wait, same day here or A&E. I'll see you in clinic in six weeks with the results, to see how the tamsulosin suits you.
[SEG0059] person_3 (PATIENT): Six weeks. I just want some sleep.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll aim for that. Reception will sort the forms. Take care, both of you.

spec.situation: Older man getting up three to four times at night, weak stream, dribbling; drinks tea in the evening; denies blood in urine; PSA and urine tests planned, tamsulosin discussed.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

omissions.text: Tamsulosin is to be taken once daily after food.
Doctor advised that tamsulosin should be stopped and the surgery contacted if the patient feels faint; recorded advice only mentions light-headedness.
Doctor warned that tamsulosin can cause light-headedness on standing, more so because the patient is also on ramipril.
Bowels and appetite were normal with no change.
Prostate examination was deferred: doctor said they would leave the prostate exam for another day.
Urine sample was intended for today if possible, with the patient saying he would try.
Doctor advised urgent same-day review or A&E if the patient cannot pass urine or sees blood in the urine; the recorded follow-up misses the A&E/same-day urgency.
Follow-up in six weeks is specifically to review the test results and how tamsulosin suits him.
